varieties.name: Black Swan
varieties.note: Rex type. Near-black leaves with a faint silver overlay. The darkest foliage needs the most light to stay compact, but burns as readily as the rest: bright shade, never sun.

varieties.name: Dark Mambo
varieties.note: Rex type. Deep purple-black with a silver spiral. Grown for the colour, which washes out towards green in a dim corner.

varieties.name: Escargot
varieties.note: Rex type. Spiralled leaf in silver and bronze. The tight whorl holds water in its centre, so water the soil and not the plant.

varieties.name: Fireworks
varieties.note: Rex type. Silver leaves with purple veining. Slower than most, and the thin leaves crisp first when the air dries.

varieties.name: Maculata
varieties.note: Cane type, the spotted angel wing. Taller, thirstier and happy in brighter light than the rex begonias these ranges are set for.

watering.label: Keep evenly moist; let only the top settle before watering again

drainage.label: Open, airy mix. The rhizome sits on the surface and rots if it stays wet

young: Too dark for a young plant. It stalls rather than grows, and the first leaves stay small.
Dim. A cutting or a fresh division will sulk here instead of rooting away.
established: Too dark. The colour washes towards plain green and the leaf stalks stretch.
Dim. New leaves come smaller than the old ones and the silver dulls.
A little short. It holds, but puts out less each time.

young: Far too much for a young plant. Thin new leaves bleach and crisp within a day.
established: Burning. The dark pigment absorbs the heat and the leaf goes papery in patches.
Too much. Colour bleaches to a flat bronze and the edges curl.
Far too much. These are forest-floor plants; direct sun scorches them through.
